transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Sofia M., Devon L., Ravi G. (Redwood) - Aisha K., Mark D., Priya P., Liam O. (Rivermark)

Summary (auto): quick update on TTFT improvements, streaming changes, sequence length trimming tests, kernel selection for ampere vs H100, and next steps.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Sofia): okay everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through the tuning work from last week - TTFT numbers, streaming behavior, and the kernel builds Devon pushed, and then sync on next steps. Aisha, did you want to start with a quick recap on the runs you did?
00:22 Speaker 2 (Aisha): yeah thanks Sofia, so we ran the 10k sample on prod-like traces, sequence lengths were a bit longer than the synthetic set, lots of short requests but a fat tail up to 512 tokens. the key point: baseline TTFT on Redwood-hosted test was about 230ms median, p95 420ms. after applying eager KV warmup + smaller batch window we saw median drop to ~200ms and p95 to 360ms. so ~12-18% improvement depending on payload.
00:58 Speaker 3 (Devon): okay that's good and matches our lab runs; we also changed the streaming handshake to send first chunk earlier - so we reduced time to first byte for streaming by shaving off the output assembly step, basically emit partial token proto as soon as token generation begins. that helped interactive feel.
01:20 Speaker 2 (Aisha): yeah i noticed the partial chunking, but one observation: some clients break on chunked JSON, so we saw a couple of parse errors in the test harness. not Redwood's fault per se but something to handle on our side.
01:35 Speaker 1 (Sofia): noted, we can send a short checklist for client tolerances - Devon, can you add recommended client backoff and a sample chunk parser?
01:44 Speaker 3 (Devon): yeah i'll drop a snippet. going back to kernels: we tested two kernel sets, the default fused-attn kernels and an experimental tiled-attn optimized for longer sequences on H100. on H100 the tiled kernels give better throughput at seq>256, but cold-start TTFT was actually slightly higher because of setup cost. on A100/ampere, fused-attn remains preferable for sub-256 sequences.
02:12 Speaker 4 (Mark): curious - what about quantization change? you mentioned 4-bit earlier, any impact on TTFT or decoding speed?
02:20 Speaker 3 (Devon): yes small impact: 4-bit reduces memory pressure and can improve throughput once loaded, but model load time slightly increases due to decode/unpack; overall TTFT can be neutral or slightly worse on first token but amortized tokens per second improves. it's a tradeoff.
02:40 Speaker 2 (Aisha): in our financial flows we care a lot about first-token latency for UI snappiness - so TTFT wins over long-run throughput for our interactive tools.
02:50 Speaker 1 (Sofia): understood, that maps to routing policy: prefer hosted low-latency variant for interactive leaderboard, fallback to quantized dedicated for batch jobs. we'll include that in the recommended routing config.
03:05 Speaker 3 (Devon): one more detail: KV cache warmup - we tried an eager cache priming step using the first 2 tokens of predictable prompts. That reduced first-generation overhead on subsequent turns. it's essentially prefix caching; benefit depends on prompt repetitiveness.
03:26 Speaker 5 (Priya): how intrusive is prefix caching for flow where prompts are semi-structured? any risk of stale state?
03:33 Speaker 3 (Devon): good question - prefix caching is purely read-only cache of key-value pairs, it's safe as long as the prompt prefix matches exactly or we use canonicalized forms. we recommend a canonicalizer on the client to normalize whitespace/tokens.
03:50 Speaker 4 (Mark): another item: kernel compilation - do you provide pre-built kernels for our private cluster or do we need to compile?
03:58 Speaker 3 (Devon): for Redwood hosted we manage kernels; for Private we can supply pre-built binaries for common flavors (H100/4-bit tiled, A100/fused). for highly-custom infra we'll provide build scripts. we'll send those scripts - note that some flags are sensitive to CUDA/toolkit versions.
04:18 Speaker 2 (Aisha): perfect, we'll need the build notes. can you include the exact nvcc/CUDA combos you validated?
04:24 Speaker 3 (Devon): yeah, I'll include nvcc 12.2 and 12.4 notes, and the driver numbers we validated.
04:32 Speaker 1 (Sofia): quick question on streaming vs chunked - any impact on cost metrics?
04:38 Speaker 3 (Devon): slightly: streaming ties up the request lifecycle longer on the server side if you hold open connections, but overall token compute is the same. in high-concurrency cases streaming can reduce perceived latency but increase concurrent connection count, so it can increase required capacity and cost if not batched smartly.
05:02 Speaker 5 (Priya): so does Redwood have suggestions for concurrency limit per customer and backpressure?
05:09 Speaker 3 (Devon): yes we have a recommended concurrency limit per model/instance type; we'll share the defaults and a pattern to ramp. also the SDK supports client-side concurrency tokens.
05:24 Speaker 2 (Aisha): on the experimental tiled kernel you mentioned p95 improvements for long seqlen - any numbers?
05:31 Speaker 3 (Devon): in lab, for seq512 the tiled kernel reduced p95 by ~22% compared to fused on H100 at the same batch config, but TTFT went up +25ms due to init. for interactive we might prefer fused on H100 too if sequences are usually <300.
05:55 Speaker 4 (Mark): ok makes sense. a practical ask: can we get a matrix of recommended kernel per sequence bucket + hardware? that would help our ops.
06:05 Speaker 1 (Sofia): noted - Devon can produce that matrix and we'll include high-level routing rules.
06:13 Speaker 6 (Liam): also want to call out network egress variance - some of our regions have higher jitter so TTFT looks worse; any mitigation?
06:22 Speaker 3 (Devon): we recommend region routing - keep interactive requests in nearest region, and fall back to cross-region only for batch. also TCP keep-alives and prewarm connections help a lot.
06:33 Speaker 2 (Aisha): on the benchmarking, we tried 100 concurrent users and a synthetic burst; curious how you recommend we do a 1k-request sweep without launching full load infra.
06:43 Speaker 3 (Devon): we'll share a lightweight script that replays traces at controlled concurrency and records per-request TTFT/latency; that's what Sofia referenced earlier.
06:51 Speaker 1 (Sofia): ok, quick recap on items and owners - Devon shares kernel flags + build scripts; Aisha runs 1k sweep; Sofia sends pricing. any blockers from Rivermark side?
07:03 Speaker 2 (Aisha): timeline is okay; small ask - can you include a short doc that maps our UI latency SLOs to recommended provisioning? for ex: SLO 200ms median TTFT -> recommended 2x reserved nodes on dedicated or hosted low-latency tier.
07:18 Speaker 1 (Sofia): yes we can create a short SLO-to-provisioning note.
07:25 Speaker 4 (Mark): another minor note - when you send the perf logs, include timestamps and instance IDs so we can correlate with our telemetry.
07:33 Speaker 3 (Devon): will do.
07:36 Speaker 5 (Priya): last thing - any licensing / compliance notes if we move private? e.g., KMS integration, audit logs?
07:44 Speaker 1 (Sofia): we have SOC2 artifacts and KMS/HSM options for private; I'll include the compliance pack and point to the security review notes from last month.
07:53 Speaker 2 (Aisha): great, thanks all.

(technical deep-dive tease)
08:05 Speaker 3 (Devon): one more micro note for the bench results - we saw occasional tail spikes correlated with GC and JIT in the runtime stack when the batcher resized; we're rolling a fix to stabilize the batch window heuristics, should land next week.
08:25 Speaker 1 (Sofia): perfect; let's close with next steps and confirm dates.
08:30 Speaker 1 (Sofia): next steps: Devon to share kernel build notes and perf scripts by 2026-03-29; Aisha to run 1k-request sweep and share logs by 2026-04-02; Sofia to send pricing by 2026-03-26. schedule deep dive tentative week of 2026-04-05. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
